'''Kenneth Eugene Iverson''' (17 December 1920 – 19 October 2004) was a Canadian [[computer scientist]] noted for the development of the [[programming language]] [[APL (programming language)|APL]]. He was honored with the [[Turing Award]] in 1979 "for his pioneering effort in programming languages and [[mathematical notation]] resulting in what the computing field now knows as APL; for his contributions to the implementation of interactive systems, to educational uses of APL, and to programming language theory and practice".<ref name=TOT/>

== Life ==
Ken Iverson was born on 17 December 1920 near [[Camrose, Alberta|Camrose]], a town in central [[Alberta]], Canada.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Campbell-Kelly |first=Martin |author-link=Martin Campbell-Kelly |date=16 November 2004 |title=Kenneth Iverson |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/kenneth-iverson-20423.html |access-date=15 December 2022 |website=[[The Independent]] |language=en}}</ref> His parents were farmers who came to Alberta from [[North Dakota]]; his ancestors came from [[Trondheim]], [[Norway]].<ref name=KEIQA/>

During [[World War II]], he served first in the [[Canadian Army]] and then in the [[Royal Canadian Air Force]].<ref name=KEIQA/><ref name=autobio/> He received a B.A. degree from [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] and the M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees from [[Harvard University]]. In his career, he worked for [[Harvard]], [[IBM]], [[I. P. Sharp Associates]], and Jsoftware Inc. (née Iverson Software Inc.).

Iverson suffered a stroke while working at the computer on a new [[J (programming language)|J]] lab on 16 October 2004,<ref>{{citation |last=Iverson |first=Eric B. |title=Dr. Kenneth E. Iverson (J Forum message) |date=21 October 2004 |url=https://jsoftware.com/pipermail/general/2004-October/018558.html |access-date=8 April 2016 |archive-date=25 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125233215/https://jsoftware.com/pipermail/general/2004-October/018558.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and died in [[Toronto]] on 19 October 2004 at age 83.<ref name=":0" />

== Education ==

Iverson began school on 1 April 1926 in a [[one-room school]],<ref name=autobio>{{citation|last1=Iverson|first1=Kenneth E.|last2=McIntyre|first2=Donald E.|title=Kenneth E. Iverson (Autobiography)|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/autobio.htm|date=2008|access-date=8 April 2016}}</ref> initially in Grade 1, promoted to Grade 2 after 3 months and to Grade 4 by the end of June 1927.
He left school after Grade 9 because it was the depths of the [[Great Depression]] and there was work to do on the [[family farm]], and because he thought further schooling only led to becoming a schoolteacher and he had no desire to become one.  At age 17, while still out of school, he enrolled in a correspondence course on radios with [[DeVry University#Early history (1931–1970)|De Forest Training]] in Chicago, and learned calculus by self-study from a textbook.<ref name=autobio/><ref>{{cite book|last1=March|first1=Herman W.|last2=Wolff|first2=Henry C.|title=Calculus|url=https://archive.org/details/calculus00marc|publisher=McGraw-Hill|year=1917}}</ref>
During [[World War II]], while serving in the [[Royal Canadian Air Force]], he took correspondence courses toward a high school diploma.

After the war, Iverson enrolled in [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in [[Kingston, Ontario]], taking advantage of government support for ex-servicemen and under threat from an Air Force buddy who said he would "beat his brains out if he did not grasp the opportunity".<ref name=autobio/> He graduated in 1950 as the top student with a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[mathematics]] and [[physics]].<ref name=KEIQA/>

Continuing his education at [[Harvard University]], he began in the Department of Mathematics and received a [[master's degree]] in 1951.  He then switched to the Department of Engineering and Applied Physics, working with [[Howard Aiken]] and [[Wassily Leontief]].

{{blockquote|Kenneth Iverson has recalled graduate study under Aiken as "like an apprenticeship" in which the student "learned the tools of the scholarship trade". Every topic was "used more as a focus for the development of skills such as clarity of thought and expression than as an end in itself". Once admitted to the program, a graduate student underwent a rite of "adoption into the fold". He was given a desk (or a share of a desk) among a group of other graduate students, the permanent staff, or visiting scholars, "most of whom were engaged in some aspect of the design and building of computers". A student was thus "made to feel part of a scholarly enterprise" and was provided, "often for the first time, with easy and intimate access to others more experienced in his chosen field".|[[I. Bernard Cohen]], ''Howard Aiken: Portrait of a Computer Pioneer'', MIT Press, 1999, page 215.<ref>{{cite book|last=Cohen|first=I. Bernard|author-link=I. Bernard Cohen|title=Howard Aiken: Portrait of a Computer Pioneer|publisher=MIT Press|date=1999|isbn=978-0-262-03262-9}}</ref>}}

{{blockquote|When interviewing Aiken, I had asked him whether Tropp and I might see his lecture notes; Aiken replied that he had always destroyed his lecture notes at the end of each year, so that he would not be tempted to repeat his lectures.|[[I. Bernard Cohen]] and Gregory W. Welch, editors, ''Makin' Numbers'', MIT Press, 1999, page xvi.<ref name=CohenII>{{cite book|editor-last1=Cohen|editor-first1=I. Bernard|editor-link1=I. Bernard Cohen|editor-last2=Welch|editor-first2=Gregory W.|title=Makin' Numbers|publisher=MIT Press|date=1999|isbn=978-0-262-03263-6}}</ref>}}

Howard Aiken had developed the [[Harvard Mark I]], one of the first large-scale digital computers, while [[Wassily Leontief]] was an economist who was developing the [[input–output model]] of economic analysis, work for which he would later receive the [[Nobel Prize]]. Leontief's model required large matrices and Iverson worked on programs that could evaluate these matrices on the [[Harvard Mark IV]] computer. Iverson received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[applied mathematics]] in 1954 with a dissertation based on this work.<ref name=PhD>{{cite thesis|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|date=1954|degree=Ph.D.|title=Machine Solutions of Linear Differential Equations – Applications to a Dynamic Economic Model|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/MSLDE.htm|institution=[[Harvard University]]|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=MSLDE|journal=Jwiki Essay|date=August 2012|url=https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Essays/MSLDE|access-date=22 April 2016}}</ref>

At Harvard, Iverson met Eoin Whitney, a 2-time [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition#Putnam Fellows|Putnam Fellow]] and fellow graduate student from Alberta.<ref>{{citation|last=Whitney|first=Arthur|author-link=Arthur Whitney (computer scientist)|title=Memories of Ken|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10010840|access-date=25 April 2016}}</ref><ref name=Cantrill/>  This had future ramifications.

== Work ==
=== Harvard (1955–1960) ===

[[File:DFSPsimplex.png|thumb|[[Simplex algorithm]] in Iverson notation<ref name=DFSP/><ref name=Montalbano>{{citation|last=Montalbano|first=Michael S.|author-link=Michael S. Montalbano|title=A Personal History of APL|date=October 1982|url=https://ed-thelen.org/comp-hist/APL-hist.html|access-date=10 April 2016}}</ref>]]

Iverson stayed on at Harvard as an [[assistant professor]] to implement the world's first graduate program in "automatic data processing".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|editor-last=Jacobson|editor-first=Arvid W.|title=Graduate Instruction and Research|journal=Proceedings of the First Conference on Training Personnel for the Computing Machine Field|publisher=Wayne State University|date=June 1954|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/GradIR.htm|access-date=9 April 2016}}</ref><ref name=APVA/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Brooks|first=Frederick P.|author-link=Fred Brooks|title=The Language, the Mind and the Man|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|page=72|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10001240|access-date=16 March 2018|archive-date=17 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180317102243/http://archive.vector.org.uk/art10001240|url-status=dead}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Many people think that Aiken was interested only in ''scientific'' computers. This was simply not so. During one coffee hour, Aiken turned to Ken Iverson, who had just finished his Ph.D., and said: "These machines are going to be immensely important for business, and I want you to prepare and teach a course in business data processing next fall." There had never been such a course anywhere in the world. Ken was qualified only because he was a mathematician. I was so excited by the prospect that I immediately volunteered to be Ken's graduate teaching assistant.|[[Fred Brooks|Frederick Brooks Jr.]], Aiken and the Harvard "Comp Lab", in I. Bernard Cohen and Gregory W. Welch, editors, ''Makin' Numbers'', MIT Press, 1999, page 141.<ref name=CohenII/>}}

It was in this period that Iverson developed notation for describing and analyzing various topics in data processing, for teaching classes, and for writing (with Brooks) ''Automatic Data Processing''.<ref name=ADP/> He was "appalled" to find that conventional mathematical notation failed to fill his needs, and began work on extensions to the notation that were more suitable.  In particular, he adopted the matrix algebra used in his thesis work, the systematic use of matrices and higher-dimensional arrays in [[tensor]] analysis, and operators in the sense of [[Oliver Heaviside|Heaviside]] in his treatment of [[Maxwell's equations]], [[higher-order function]]s on function argument(s) with a function result.<ref name=autobio/>  The notation was also field-tested in the business world in 1957 during a 6-month sabbatical spent at [[McKinsey & Company]].<ref name=autobio/><ref name=APLEvol>{{cite journal|last1=Falkoff|first1=Adin D.|author-link1=Adin Falkoff|last2=Iverson|first2=Kenneth E.|title=The Evolution of APL|journal=ACM SIGPLAN Notices|volume=13|issue=8|date=August 1978|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLEvol.htm|access-date=9 April 2016|doi=10.1145/960118.808372|pages=47–57|s2cid=6050177|doi-access=free}}</ref> The first published paper using the notation was ''The Description of Finite Sequential Processes'', initially Report Number 23 to [[Bell Labs]] and later revised and presented at the Fourth London Symposium on Information Theory in August 1960.<ref name=DFSP>{{citation|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=The Description of Finite Sequential Processes|journal=Symposium on Information Theory|publisher=Royal Institution, London|date=August 1960|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/DFSP.htm|access-date=9 April 2016}}</ref><ref name=JKT/>

Iverson stayed at Harvard for five years but failed to get tenure, because "[he hadn't] published anything but the one little book".<ref name=KEIQA>{{citation|editor-last=Hui|editor-first=Roger|editor-link=Roger Hui|title=Ken Iverson Quotations and Anecdotes|date=30 September 2005|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/KEIQA.htm|access-date=12 February 2019}}</ref>

=== IBM (1960–1980) ===

Iverson joined [[IBM Research]] in 1960 (and doubled his salary).<ref name=autobio/> He was preceded to IBM by [[Fred Brooks]], who advised him to "stick to whatever [he] really wanted to do, because management was so starved for ideas that anything not clearly crazy would find support." In particular, he was allowed to finish and publish ''A Programming Language''<ref name=JKT>{{citation|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=Letter to J.K. Tuttle|date=14 December 1983|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/JKTletter.htm|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref><ref name=APL>{{cite book|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=A Programming Language|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|date=1962|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APL.htm|access-date=9 April 2016}} {{isbn|978-0-471-43014-8|}}.</ref> and (with Brooks) ''Automatic Data Processing'',<ref name=ADP>{{cite book|last1=Brooks Jr.|first1=Frederick P.|author-link1=Fred Brooks|last2=Iverson|first2=Kenneth E.|title=Automatic Data Processing|publisher=Wiley|date=1963}} {{isbn|978-0-471-10599-2}}.</ref> two books that described and used the notation developed at Harvard.  (''Automatic Data Processing'' and ''A Programming Language'' began as one book "but the material grew in both magnitude and level until a separation proved wise".<ref name=ADP/><ref name=APL/>)

At IBM, Iverson soon met [[Adin Falkoff]], and they worked together for the next twenty years.  Chapter 2 of ''A Programming Language'' used Iverson's notation to describe the [[IBM 7090]] computer.<ref name=JKT/><ref name=APL/>  In early 1963 Falkoff, later joined by Iverson and [[Edward H. Sussenguth|Ed Sussenguth]], proceeded to use the notation to produce a formal description of the [[IBM System/360]] computer then under design.<ref name=APLDesign>{{cite journal|last1=Falkoff|first1=Adin D.|author-link1=Adin Falkoff|last2=Iverson|first2=Kenneth E.|title=The Design of APL|journal=IBM Journal of Research and Development|volume=17|number=4|date=July 1973|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLDesign.htm|access-date=9 April 2016|doi=10.1147/rd.174.0324|doi-access=free|pages=324–334|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The result was published in 1964 in a double issue of the IBM Systems Journal,<ref name=desc360>{{cite journal|last1=Falkoff|first1=Adin D.|author-link1=Adin Falkoff|last2=Iverson|first2=Kenneth E.|last3=Sussenguth|first3=Edward H.|author-link3=Edward H. Sussenguth|title=A Formal Description of System/360|journal=IBM Systems Journal|volume=3|number=3|date=1964|url=https://www.research.ibm.com/journal/sj/032/falkoff.pdf|doi=10.1147/sj.32.0198|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060813132807/https://www.research.ibm.com/journal/sj/032/falkoff.pdf|archive-date=13 August 2006|pages=198–261}}</ref> thereafter known as the "grey book" or "grey manual". The book was used in a course on computer systems design at the IBM Systems Research Institute.<ref name=desc360/> A consequence of the formal description was that it attracted the interest of bright young minds.<ref name=autobio/><ref name=APLQA>{{citation|editor-last=Hui|editor-first=Roger|editor-link=Roger Hui|title=APL Quotations and Anecdotes|date=September 2010|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#APL_birthday|access-date=9 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705152219/https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#APL_birthday|archive-date=5 July 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> One hotbed of interest was at [[Stanford University]] which included [[Lawrence M. Breed|Larry Breed]], [[Philip S. Abrams|Phil Abrams]], [[Roger Moore (computer scientist)|Roger Moore]], [[Charles Brenner (mathematician)|Charles Brenner]],<ref name=IBM1130/> and Mike Jenkins,<ref>{{citation|last=Jenkins|first=Michael A.|title=The Solution of Linear Systems of Equations and Linear Least Squares Problems in APL|journal=Technical Report Number 320-2989|publisher=IBM Corp.|date=June 1970}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Jenkins|first=Michael A.|title=Domino – An APL Primitive Function for Matrix Inverse – Its Implementation and Applications|date=10 February 1972|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=3|number=4}} Reprinted in {{citation |doi=10.1145/1115910.1115911 |doi-access=free |title=DOMINO: An APL Primitive Function for Matrix Inversion – – Its Implementation and Applications |date=1972 |last1=Jenkins |first1=M. A. |journal=ACM SIGPLAN Notices |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=29–40 }}</ref> all of whom later made contributions to APL. Donald McIntyre, head of geology at [[Pomona College]] which had the first general customer installation of a 360 system, used the formal description to become more expert than the IBM systems engineer assigned to Pomona.<ref name=autobio/><ref name=DBM>{{citation|last=McIntyre|first=Donald B.|title=A Tribute to Ken Iverson|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10005900|access-date=25 April 2016}}</ref>

With the completion of the formal description Falkoff and Iverson turned their attention to implementation. This work was brought to rapid fruition in 1965 when [[Lawrence M. Breed|Larry Breed]] and [[Philip S. Abrams|Phil Abrams]] joined the project.  They produced a FORTRAN-based implementation on the 7090 called IVSYS (for Iverson system) by autumn 1965, first in batch mode and later, in early 1966, in time-shared interactive mode.<ref name=IBM1130/><ref name=IBMfamily>{{cite journal|last=Falkoff|first=Adin D.|author-link=Adin Falkoff|title=The IBM Family of APL Systems|journal=IBM Systems Journal|volume=30|number=4|date=December 1991|doi=10.1147/sj.304.0416|pages=416–432}}</ref><ref name=Abrams>{{citation|last=Abrams|first=Philip S.|author-link=Philip S. Abrams|title=An Interpreter for "Iverson Notation"|journal=Technical Report: CS-TR-66-47|publisher=Department of Computer Science, Stanford University|date=17 August 1966|url=https://i.stanford.edu/pub/cstr/reports/cs/tr/66/47/CS-TR-66-47.pdf|access-date=17 April 2016|archive-date=30 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150930181454/http://i.stanford.edu/pub/cstr/reports/cs/tr/66/47/CS-TR-66-47.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Subsequently, Breed, [[Richard H. Lathwell|Dick Lathwell]] (ex [[University of Alberta]]), and Roger Moore (of [[I. P. Sharp Associates]]) produced the System/360 implementation;<ref name=APL360>{{citation|last1=Falkoff|first1=Adin D.|author-link1=Adin Falkoff|last2=Iverson|first2=Kenneth E.|title=The APL\360 Terminal System|date=16 October 1967|journal=Research Report RC-1922|publisher=IBM|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APL360TerminalSystem.htm|access-date=9 April 2016}}</ref> the three received the [[Grace Murray Hopper Award]] in 1973 "for their work in the design and implementation of APL\360, setting new standards in simplicity, efficiency, reliability and response time for interactive systems."<ref>ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award (1973): [https://awards.acm.org/award_winners/breed_0694605.cfm Breed], [https://awards.acm.org/award_winners/lathwell_3412588.cfm Lathwell], and [https://awards.acm.org/award_winners/moore_4987585.cfm Moore]; retrieved 14 April 2016.</ref> While the 360 implementation work was underway "Iverson notation"<ref name=Abrams/><ref>{{cite book|last=Horvath|first=Robert W.|title=Introduction to Iverson Notation|date=August 1966|publisher=IBM Systems Development Division, Poughkeepsie, NY}}</ref> was renamed "APL", by Falkoff.<ref name=sourcebook>{{citation|editor-last=McDonnell|editor-first=Eugene|editor-link=Eugene McDonnell|title=A Source Book in APL, Introduction|publisher=APL Press|date=1981|url=https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Doc/A_Source_Book_in_APL|access-date=19 April 2016}}</ref> The workspace "1 cleanspace" was saved at 1966-11-27 22.53.58 [[Coordinated Universal Time|UTC]].<ref name=APLQA/> APL\360 service began within IBM several weeks before that<ref>{{citation|last=Breed|first=Larry|author-link=Lawrence M. Breed|title=The First APL Terminal Session|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=22|number=1|date=September 1991|pages=2–4|doi=10.1145/138094.140933|s2cid=43138444|doi-access=free}}</ref> and outside IBM in 1968.<ref name=IBMfamily/> Additional information on the implementation of APL\360 can be found in the Acknowledgements of the ''APL\360 User's Manual''<ref name=APL360user/> and in "Appendix. Chronology of APL development" of ''The Design of APL''.<ref name=APLDesign/>

[[File:APLparen.png|thumb|APL expression for the depth of parentheses nesting<ref name=amuse>{{citation|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=Sixteen APL Amuse-Bouches|date=11 October 2014|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/amuse-bouches.htm|access-date=12 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Perlis|first=Alan J.|author-link=Alan Perlis|title=Almost Perfect Artifacts Improve only in Small Ways: APL is more French than English|journal=APL 78 Conference Proceedings|date=29 March 1978|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/perlis78.htm|access-date=12 April 2016}}</ref>]]

The formal description and especially the implementation drove the evolution of the language, a process of consolidation and regularization in typography, linearization, syntax, and function definition described in ''APL\360 History'',<ref name=APLHist>{{citation|last=Falkoff|first=Adin D.|author-link=Adin Falkoff|title=APL\360 History|journal=Proceedings of the APL Users Conference at SUNY Binghamton|date=July 1969|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/apl360history.htm|access-date=9 April 2016}}</ref> ''The Design of APL'',<ref name=APLDesign/> and ''The Evolution of APL''.<ref name=APLEvol/> Two treatises from this period, ''Conventions Governing the Order of Evaluation''<ref>{{citation|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=Conventions Governing Order of Evaluation (Appendix A of Elementary Functions: An Algorithmic Treatment)|publisher=Science Research Associates|date=1966|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/EvalOrder.htm|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref> and ''Algebra as a Language'',<ref>{{citation|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=Algebra as a Language (Appendix A of Algebra: An Algorithmic Treatment)|publisher=Addison-Wesley|date=1972|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/algebra.htm|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref> are apologias of APL notation.

The notation was used by Falkoff and Iverson to teach various topics at various universities and at the IBM Systems Research Institute.<ref name=APLDesign/><ref name=APLHist/> In 1964 Iverson used the notation in a one-semester course for seniors at the [[Fox Lane High School]],<ref name=sourcebook/><ref name=fns>{{cite book|last=Iverson|first=Kenneth E.|title=Elementary Functions: An Algorithmic Treatment|date=March 1966|publisher=Science Research Associates}}</ref> and later in [[Swarthmore High School]].<ref name=autobio/> After APL became available its first application was to teach formal methods in systems design at [[Goddard Space Flight Center|NASA Goddard]].<ref name=APLHist/><ref>{{citation|last=McDonnell|first=Eugene|author-link=Eugene McDonnell|title=The Socio-Technical Beginnings of APL|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=10|number=2|date=December 1979|page=13|doi=10.1145/586148.586155|s2cid=18025422|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/eem/socio.htm|access-date=24 April 2016|doi-access=free}}</ref> It was also used at the [[Hotchkiss School]],<ref name=IBM1130>{{cite journal|last=Breed|first=Larry|author-link=Lawrence M. Breed|title=How We Got to APL\1130|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10001190|access-date=13 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160318185611/http://archive.vector.org.uk/art10001190|archive-date=18 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Lower Canada College]],<ref>{{citation|last=Goldsmith|first=Leslie H.|title=APL Quotations and Anecdotes|editor-last=Hui|editor-first=Roger|editor-link=Roger Hui|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#666box|access-date=13 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705152219/https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#666box|archive-date=5 July 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Scotch Plains-Fanwood High School|Scotch Plains High School]],<ref>{{cite journal|last=McDonnell|first=Eugene|author-link=Eugene McDonnell|title=Recreational APL, Pyramigram|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=11|number=1|date=September 1980|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/eem/qq111.htm|access-date=13 April 2016}}</ref> Atlanta public schools,<ref>{{citation|author=<!-- Unstated on webpage. -->|title=APL in the Atlanta Public Schools|date=October 1969|journal=SHARE*APL\360 Newsletter|number=3}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=APL IV: Fourth International APL Conference|date=June 1972|url=https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED074766|access-date=29 April 2016}}</ref> among others. In one school the students became so eager that they broke into the school after hours to get more APL computer time;<ref name=APLQA/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Biancuzzi|first1=Federico|last2=Warden|first2=Shane|title=Masterminds of Programming|publisher=O'Reilly Media|date=March 2009|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#Falkoff|access-date=13 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705152219/https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/APLQA.htm#Falkoff|archive-date=5 July 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> in another the APL enthusiasts steered newbies to [[BASIC]] so as to maximize their own APL time.<ref name=IBM1130/>

In 1969, Iverson and the APL group inaugurated the IBM Philadelphia Scientific Center.<ref name=IBMfamily/><ref name=APLHist/> In 1970 he was named [[IBM Fellow]].<ref name=Goode/> He used the funding that came with being an IBM Fellow to bring in visiting teachers and professors from various fields, including Donald McIntyre from  Pomona<ref name=DBM/> and [[Jeffrey Shallit|Jeff Shallit]] as a summer student.<ref name=APLQA/> For a period of several months the visitors would start using APL for expositions in their own fields, and the hope was that later they would continue their use of APL at their home institutions.<ref>{{citation|last=Berry|first=Paul|title=Expository Programming|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10000980|access-date=25 April 2015}}</ref> Iverson's work at this time centered in several disciplines, including collaborative projects in circuit theory, genetics, geology, and calculus.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Berry|first1=Paul |last2=Bartoli|first2=G.|last3=Dell'Aquila|first3=C. |last4=Spadavecchia|first4=V.|title=APL and Insight|journal=TR No. CRB 002/513-3502|publisher=IBM Corp.|date=March 1973}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Spence|first=Robert|title=Resistive Circuit Theory|publisher=IBM|date=March 1973}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Orth|first=Donald L.|title=Calculus in a New Key|publisher=APL Press|date=1976|isbn=978-0-917326-05-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Berry|first1=Paul|last2=Thorstensen|first2=John|title=Starmap|journal=TR No. 02.665|publisher=IBM Corp.|date=1973}}</ref> When the PSC closed in 1974,<ref name=IBMfamily/><ref name=sourcebook/> some of the group transferred to California while others including Iverson remained in the East, later transferring back to IBM Research. He received the [[Turing Award]] in 1979.<ref name=TOT/>

=== I. P. Sharp Associates (1980–1987) ===

[[File:APLrank.png|thumb|APL rank operator ⍤ <ref name=SAX/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=On Average|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=4|date=August 2010|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10500270|access-date=12 April 2016}}</ref>]]

In 1980, Iverson left IBM for [[I. P. Sharp Associates]],<ref>{{cite journal|author=IPSA|title=Dr. Kenneth E. Iverson|journal=The I.P. Sharp Newsletter|volume=8|number=1|date=January 1980|access-date=8 August 2019|url=https://www.snakeisland.com/IPSANewsletter_1980_01_02.pdf}}</ref><ref name=EEMQA>{{citation|editor-last=Hui|editor-first=Roger|editor-link=Roger Hui|title=Eugene McDonnell Quotations and Anecdotes|date=14 May 2009|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/eem/anecdotes.htm#ebi1|access-date=5 April 2016}}</ref> an APL [[time-sharing]] company.  He was preceded there by his IBM colleagues Paul Berry, Joey Tuttle, [[Richard H. Lathwell|Dick Lathwell]], and [[Eugene McDonnell]].  At IPSA, the APL language and systems group was managed by Eric Iverson (Ken Iverson's son); [[Roger Moore (computer scientist)|Roger Moore]], one of the APL\360 implementers, was a vice president.

Iverson worked to develop and extend APL on the lines presented in ''Operators and Functions''.<ref name=opfns/><ref name=APL1978>{{cite journal|last1=Hui|first1=Roger|last2=Kromberg|first2=Morten|title=APL Since 1978|journal=Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages|volume=4|number=HOPL|date=June 2020|pages=1–108|doi=10.1145/3386319|s2cid=218517570|doi-access=free}}</ref> The language work gained impetus in 1981 when [[Arthur Whitney (computer scientist)|Arthur Whitney]] and Iverson produced a model of APL written in APL<ref name=APLmodel/><ref name=APLSyntaxSemantics/> at the same time they were working on IPSA's [[OAG (company)|OAG]] database.<ref name=KEIQA/><ref name=Cantrill>{{cite journal|last=Cantrill|first=Bryan|author-link=Bryan Cantrill|title=A Conversation with Arthur Whitney|journal=ACM Queue|volume=7|number=2|date=February 2009|url=https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=1531242|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{citation|author=<!-- Unstated on webpage. -->|title=A Celebration of Kenneth Iverson|publisher=[[Computer History Museum]]|date=30 November 2004|url=https://keiapl.org/rhui/passage.htm#museum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721154034/http://keiapl.org/rhui/passage.htm#museum|url-status=usurped|archive-date=21 July 2011|access-date=17 April 2016}}</ref> (Iverson introduced Arthur Whitney, son of Eoin Whitney, to APL when he was 11 years old<ref name=Cantrill/> and in 1974 recommended him for a summer student position at IPSA [[Calgary]].<ref name=APLQA/>) In the model, the APL syntax was driven by an 11-by-5 table.  Whitney also invented the [[Rank (J programming language)|rank operator]] in the process.<ref name=KEIrem>{{citation|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=Remembering Ken Iverson|url=https://keiapl.org/rhui/remember.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080606130709/http://keiapl.org/rhui/remember.htm|url-status=usurped|archive-date=6 June 2008|date=November 2014|access-date=10 April 2016}}</ref> The language design was further simplified and extended in ''Rationalized APL''<ref name=RatAPL/> in January 1983, multiple editions of ''A Dictionary of the APL Language'' between 1984 and 1987, and ''A Dictionary of APL''<ref name=APLDict/> in September 1987. Within IPSA, the phrase "dictionary APL" came into use to denote the APL specified by ''A Dictionary of APL'', itself referred to as "the dictionary".  In the dictionary, APL syntax is controlled by a 9-by-6 table and the parsing process was precisely and succinctly described in Table 2, and there is a primitive (monadic ⊥, modeled in APL) for word formation ([[Lexical analysis|lexing]]).

In the 1970s and 1980s, the main APL vendors were [[IBM]], [[Scientific Time Sharing Corporation|STSC]], and [[I.P. Sharp Associates|IPSA]], and all three were active in developing and extending the language. IBM had APL2, based on the work of [[Jim Brown (computer scientist)|Jim Brown]].<ref>{{cite thesis|last=Brown|first=James A.|author-link=Jim Brown (computer scientist)|title=A Generalization of APL|degree=Ph.D.|publisher=Department of Computer and Information Sciences, Syracuse University|date=1971}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Brown|first=James A.|author-link=Jim Brown (computer scientist)|title=The Principles of APL2|journal=Technical Report 03.247|publisher=IBM Santa Teresa Laboratory|date=1984}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Brown|first=James A.|author-link=Jim Brown (computer scientist)|title=APL2 Programming: Language Reference|journal=Sh20-9227|publisher=IBM Corporation|date=1988}}</ref> Work on APL2 proceeded intermittently for 15 years,<ref name=IBMfamily/> with actual coding starting in 1971 and APL2 becoming available as an IUP (Installed User Program, an IBM product classification) in 1982. STSC had an experimental APL system called NARS, designed and implemented by Bob Smith.<ref>{{citation|doi=10.1145/800142.805376|doi-access=free |chapter=Nested arrays, operators, and functions |title=Proceedings of the international conference on APL - APL '81 |date=1981 |last1=Smith |first1=Bob |pages=286–290 |isbn=0-89791-035-4 }}</ref><ref name=NARS>{{citation|last=Cheney|first=Carl M.|title=APL*PLUS Nested Array System|publisher=[[Scientific Time Sharing Corporation|STSC, Inc.]]|date=1981|url=https://www.sudleyplace.com/APL/Nested%20Arrays%20System.pdf|access-date=19 April 2016}}</ref> NARS and APL2 differed in fundamental respects from dictionary APL,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Orth|first=Donald L.|title=A Comparison of the IPSA and STSC Implementations of Operators and General Arrays|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=12|number=2|date=December 1981|page=11|doi=10.1145/586656.586662|doi-access=free|s2cid=1642446|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/IPSA_STSC.htm|access-date=13 April 2016}}</ref> and differed from each other.

I.P. Sharp implemented the new APL ideas in stages: complex numbers,<ref name=SATN40>{{cite journal|last=McDonnell|first=Eugene|author-link=Eugene McDonnell|title=Complex Numbers |journal=SHARP APL Technical Note|volume=40 |date=20 June 1981|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/satn40.htm|access-date=11 April 2016}}</ref> enclosed (boxed) arrays, match, and composition operators in 1981,<ref name=SATN41/> the determinant operator in 1982,<ref name=SATN42/> and the rank operator, link, and the left and right identity functions in 1983.<ref name=SATN45/> However, the domains of operators were still restricted to the primitive functions or subsets thereof. In 1986, IPSA developed SAX,<ref name=SAX>{{cite book|last=Steinbrook|first=David H.|title=SAX Reference|year=1986|publisher=[[I. P. Sharp Associates]]}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Tuttle|first=Joey K.|title=What's Wrong with My Programming?|journal=Vector|volume=22|number=3|date=August 2006|url=https://archive.vector.org.uk/art10010720|access-date=25 April 2016}}</ref> SHARP APL/Unix, written in C and based on an implementation by [[Scientific Time Sharing Corporation|STSC]]. The language was as specified in the dictionary with no restrictions on the domains of operators.  An alpha version of SAX became available within I.P. Sharp around December 1986 or early 1987.

In education, Iverson developed ''A SHARP APL Minicourse''<ref name=inductive/><ref name=mini/> used to teach IPSA clients in the use of APL, and ''Applied Mathematics for Programmers''<ref name=AMFP/> and ''Mathematics and Programming''<ref name=MAP/> which were used in computer science courses at [[University of Twente|T.H. Twente]].

=== Jsoftware (1990–2004) ===

[[File:Jbinomial.png|thumb|J [[Tacit programming|tacit verb]] for binomial coefficients<ref name=amuse/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=Ken Iverson's Favorite APL Expression?|journal=Dyalog Blog|date=3 December 2014|url=https://www.dyalog.com/blog/2014/12/ken-iversons-favourite-apl-expression/|access-date=12 April 2016}}</ref>]]

[[File:APLbinomial.png|thumb|Dyalog APL<ref>{{citation|author=<!-- Unstated on webpage. -->|title=Dyalog APL Language Reference (version 14.0 or later)|publisher=Dyalog Limited|date=2014|url=https://docs.dyalog.com/14.1/Dyalog%20APL%20Language%20Reference.pdf|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref> equivalent computation]]

Iverson retired from I. P. Sharp Associates in 1987.  He kept busy while "between jobs".  Regarding language design, the most significant of his activities in this period was the invention of "fork" in 1988.<ref name=fork/>  For years, he had struggled to find a way to write f+g as in calculus, from the "scalar operators" in 1978,<ref name=opfns/> through the "til" operator in 1982,<ref name=APLmodel/><ref name=RatAPL/> the catenation and reshape operators in 1984,<ref name=OpCalculus/> the union and intersection operators in 1987,<ref name=APLDict/> "yoke" in 1988,<ref name=APLCommentary/> and finally forks in 1988. Forks are defined as follows:

{|
|-
| &nbsp; &nbsp;||&nbsp; (f g h) y||&nbsp; ←→ &nbsp;||(f y) g (h y)
|-
| &nbsp; &nbsp;||x (f g h) y||&nbsp; ←→ &nbsp;||(x f y) g (x h y)
|}

Moreover, (f g p q r) ←→ (f g (p q r)). Thus to write f+g as in calculus, one can write f+g in APL. Iverson and [[Eugene McDonnell]] worked out the details on the long plane rides to the APL88 conference in Sydney, Australia, with Iverson coming up with the initial idea on waking up from a nap.<ref name=KEIrem/><ref>{{citation|last=Hodgkinson|first=Rob|title=J Programming Forum post|url=https://jsoftware.com/pipermail/programming/2017-October/049330.html|date=19 October 2017|access-date=22 June 2018|archive-date=5 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200205231442/http://jsoftware.com/pipermail/programming/2017-October/049330.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=APL1978/>{{rp|§1.3,§3.8}}

Iverson presented the rationale for his work post 1987 as follows:<ref name=APVA/>

{{blockquote|When I retired from paid employment, I turned my attention back to this matter [the use of APL for teaching] and soon concluded that the essential tool required was a dialect of APL that:
:• Is available as "shareware", and is inexpensive enough to be acquired by students as well as by schools
:• Can be printed on standard printers
:• Runs on a wide variety of computers
:• Provides the simplicity and the generality of the latest thinking in APL

The result has been [[J (programming language)|J]], first reported in [the ''APL 90 Conference Proceedings''].<ref name=J1990/>}}

[[Roger Hui]] described the final impetus that got J started in Appendix A of ''An Implementation of J'':<ref name=AIOJ>{{cite book|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|date=27 January 1992|title=An Implementation of J|publisher=Iverson Software Inc.|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/books/pdf/aioj.pdf|access-date=10 April 2016}}</ref>

{{blockquote|One summer weekend in 1989, [[Arthur Whitney (computer scientist)|Arthur Whitney]] visited Ken Iverson at Kiln Farm and produced—on one page and in one afternoon—an interpreter fragment on the [[AT&T UNIX PC|AT&T 3B1 computer]]. I studied this interpreter for about a week for its organization and programming style; and on Sunday, August 27, 1989, at about four o'clock in the afternoon, wrote the first line of code that became the implementation described in this document.

Arthur's one-page interpreter fragment is as follows: ...}}

Hui, a classmate of Whitney at the [[University of Alberta]], had studied ''A Dictionary of the APL Language'' when ''he'' was between jobs,<ref name=autobio/> modelled the parsing process in at least two different ways,<ref name=KEIrem/> and investigated uses of dictionary APL in diverse applications.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=Some Uses of { and }|journal=APL 87 Conference Proceedings|date=May 1987|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/from.htm|access-date=15 April 2016}}</ref> As well, from January 1987 to August 1989 he had access to SAX,<ref name=SAX/> and in the later part of that period used it on a daily basis.<ref name=KEIrem/>

J initially took ''A Dictionary of APL''<ref name=APLDict/> as the specification, and the J interpreter was built around Table 2 of the dictionary. The C data and program structures were designed so that the parse table in C corresponded directly to the parse table in the dictionary.<ref name=KEIrem/>  In retrospect, Iverson's APL87 paper ''APL87'',<ref name=APL87/> in five pages, prescribed all the essential steps in writing an APL interpreter, in particular the sections on word formation and parsing.  [[Arthur Whitney (computer scientist)|Arthur Whitney]], in addition to the "one-page thing", contributed to J development by suggesting that primitives be oriented on the leading axis, that agreement (a generalization of scalar extension) should be prefix instead of suffix,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=Rank and Uniformity|journal=APL 95 Conference Proceedings|date=June 1995|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/rank.htm|access-date=15 April 2016}}</ref> and that a total array ordering be defined.<ref>{{citation|last=Hui|first=Roger|author-link=Roger Hui|title=The TAO of J|journal=J Wiki Essay|date=27 January 2006|url=https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Essays/The_TAO_of_J|access-date=24 May 2016}}</ref>

One of the objectives was to implement fork. This turned out to be rather straightforward, by the inclusion of one additional row in the parse table. The choice to implement forks was fortuitous and fortunate. It was realized only later<ref name=tacit/><ref>{{cite book|last=Cherlin|first=Edward|title=Proceedings of the international conference on APL '91 - APL '91 |chapter=Pure functions in APL and J |date=August 1991|pages=88–93 |doi=10.1145/114054.114065 |doi-access=free |isbn=0897914414 |s2cid=25802202 }}</ref> that forks made [[Tacit programming|tacit expressions]] (operator expressions) complete in the following sense: any sentence involving one or two arguments that did not use its arguments as an operand, can be written tacitly with fork, compose, the left and right identity functions, and constant functions.

Two obvious differences between J and other APL dialects are: (a) its use of terms from natural languages instead of from mathematics or computer science (the practice began with ''A Dictionary of APL''): noun, verb, adverbs, alphabet, word formation, sentence, ... instead of array, function, operator, character set, lexing, expression, ... ; and (b) its use of 7-bit ASCII characters instead of special symbols.  Other differences between J and APL are described in ''J for the APL Programmer''<ref name=JFA>{{cite journal|last1=Burke|first1=Chris|last2=Hui|first2=Roger|author-link2=Roger Hui|title=J for the APL Programmer|journal=APL Quote Quad|volume=27|number=1|date=September 1996|pages=11–17|doi=10.1145/1151395.1151400|s2cid=9203778|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/j4apl.htm|access-date=14 April 2016|doi-access=free}}</ref> and ''APL and J''.<ref>{{citation|last=Burke|first=Chris|title=APL and J|date=2 March 2005|url=https://www.jsoftware.com/papers/aplj.pdf|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref>

The J source code is available from Jsoftware under the [[GNU General Public License]] version 3 (GPL3), or a commercial alternative.<ref>{{citation|author=<!-- Unstated on webpage. -->|title=J Source|url=https://jsoftware.com/source.htm|publisher=Jsoftware, Inc.|access-date=15 April 2016|archive-date=22 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422071010/http://www.jsoftware.com/source.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Eric Iverson founded Iverson Software Inc., in February 1990 to provide an improved SHARP APL/PC product. It quickly became obvious that there were shared interests and goals, and in May 1990 Iverson and Hui joined Iverson Software Inc.; later joined by Chris Burke. The company soon became J only. The name was changed to Jsoftware Inc., in April 2000.<ref name=KEIrem/>

[[File:KEI&Hui.jpg|thumb|Ken Iverson (right) and Roger Hui, 1996]]
